unit.title: Forces and Motion
unit.essential_question: How do forces affect the motion of objects, and how can we represent those forces?

official_assessment_targets.title: 1.1 The Language of Physics
official_assessment_targets.learning_target: Understand how physicists describe, measure, and explain the natural world using models, experiments, and evidence.
i_cans: U1-S1-IC1: distinguish observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory
U1-S1-IC2: explain why a scientific claim must be testable
U1-S1-IC3: use evidence from a short scenario to determine the supported explanation and explain that formulas are guides for thinking, not just calculation

official_assessment_targets.title: 1.2 Newton’s First Law
official_assessment_targets.learning_target: Explain how inertia affects motion and apply Newton’s First Law to objects at rest or moving at constant velocity.
i_cans: U1-S2-IC1: state Newton’s First Law in everyday language
U1-S2-IC2: explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force
U1-S2-IC3: distinguish no forces acting from no net force acting and identify support force, weight, and other common forces

official_assessment_targets.title: 1.3 Describing and Combining Forces
official_assessment_targets.learning_target: Represent forces as vectors and determine the combined effect when multiple forces act.
i_cans: U1-S3-IC1: explain that force is a vector
U1-S3-IC2: combine forces in the same and opposite directions
U1-S3-IC3: identify resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare forces

official_assessment_targets.title: 1.4 Equilibrium and Mechanical Equilibrium
official_assessment_targets.learning_target: Explain when forces are balanced and how equilibrium relates to object motion.
i_cans: U1-S4-IC1: distinguish static and dynamic equilibrium
U1-S4-IC2: explain that an object at rest can still have forces acting on it
U1-S4-IC3: explain that an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule for up/down/left/right forces

official_assessment_targets.title: 1.5 Drawing Force Diagrams
official_assessment_targets.learning_target: Create and interpret simple force diagrams and use them to explain and predict motion.
i_cans: U1-S5-IC1: draw a force diagram for a real-world object
U1-S5-IC2: decide whether forces are balanced or unbalanced
U1-S5-IC3: explain the effect of net force on motion and critique or revise an incorrect force explanation

whole_unit_progression: Use observation, evidence, testability, models, and relationships to describe physical situations.
Develop Newton’s First Law as the no-change condition and separate inertia from force.
Represent individual forces as vectors and combine them into a resultant or net force.
Treat equilibrium as the special case of zero net force, including both rest and constant-velocity motion.
Transfer the full model into force diagrams that identify the system, external forces, net force, and motion prediction.

sections.title: 1.1 The Language of Physics
sections.learning_target: Understand how physicists describe, measure, and explain the natural world using models, experiments, and evidence.

student_facing.purpose: Establish the evidence-and-model language students will use throughout the force unit.
concept_sequence: formulas as relationships that describe a phenomenon

worked_examples.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording, answer choices/response structure, solution, and any Bank figure exactly at Stage 4B; use as the guided Example for this section.

you_try.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording and representation exactly at Stage 4B; pair with the worked example as same-I-can transfer.

wtc.placement: after students have separated observation from inference and discussed testability
wtc.instruction: Use canonical wording exactly; do not paraphrase the Bank item.

item_lenses: relationships/formulas communicate physical structure rather than serving only as answer machines

misconceptions: an inference is the same as an observation
a theory is merely a guess
a formula is only a calculation recipe
questions: What was directly measured or seen?
What conclusion goes beyond the observation?
What evidence could make the claim testable?
teacher_only.answer_visibility: Keep Bank answers and solution reasoning teacher-only except where the PM explicitly calls for a worked Example.
teacher_only.worked_notes: Narrate how evidence constrains the explanation; do not introduce new example content outside the Bank.
teacher_only.wtc_interpretation: Use the WTC as a transfer from vocabulary to an unfamiliar evidence set.

sections.title: 1.2 Newton’s First Law
sections.learning_target: Explain how inertia affects motion and apply Newton’s First Law to objects at rest or moving at constant velocity.

student_facing.purpose: Replace the everyday idea that motion requires a continuing push with the Newton’s First Law model.
concept_sequence: inertia as a property of matter
Newton’s First Law in everyday language
zero net force and constant velocity
common forces: weight, support, applied force, friction
no forces versus no net force

worked_examples.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording, solution, and representation exactly at Stage 4B.

you_try.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording and representation exactly; preserve same-I-can progression.

representation_progression: WTC transfer with balanced horizontal forces
item_lenses: constant velocity does not mean no forces
zero net force is the relevant condition

misconceptions: a moving object must have a forward force
if net force is zero then no forces act
questions: What does Newton’s First Law predict if net force remains zero?
teacher_only.answer_visibility: Do not expose downstream Bank answers in student prompts.
teacher_only.worked_notes: Keep the conceptual no-change condition primary; equations are secondary.
teacher_only.wtc_interpretation: Use the WTC to connect equal opposing forces to unchanged motion.

sections.title: 1.3 Describing and Combining Forces
sections.learning_target: Represent forces as vectors and determine the combined effect when multiple forces act.

student_facing.purpose: Move from naming forces to representing magnitude and direction and combining them into one resultant effect.

worked_examples.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording, vector representation, and solution exactly at Stage 4B.

you_try.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording and vector representation exactly; use as reduced-support transfer.

wtc.placement: after students can combine collinear force vectors

representation_progression: WTC transfer where direction changes the result
item_lenses: magnitude is encoded by arrow length
direction is part of the quantity
net force is a vector result, not just a numerical sum

misconceptions: all force magnitudes should simply be added
arrow location alone determines force magnitude
net force has magnitude but no direction
questions: What does the arrow length communicate?
Which directions reinforce and which oppose?
What single vector has the same overall effect?
teacher_only.answer_visibility: Keep resultants/solutions hidden on student-facing practice diagrams unless it is the worked Example.
teacher_only.wtc_interpretation: Use WTC as a check that students attach direction to the numerical resultant.

sections.title: 1.4 Equilibrium and Mechanical Equilibrium
sections.learning_target: Explain when forces are balanced and how equilibrium relates to object motion.

student_facing.purpose: Generalize zero net force into equilibrium and distinguish static from dynamic equilibrium.
concept_sequence: balanced forces and zero net force
objects at rest can have forces
constant straight-line velocity can be equilibrium

worked_examples.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording, solution, and representation exactly at Stage 4B.

you_try.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording and representation exactly; use as same-I-can transfer.

wtc.placement: after static and dynamic equilibrium have both been established

representation_progression: WTC transfer from equilibrium to changed net force
item_lenses: equilibrium means zero net force, not necessarily zero velocity
ΣF=0 is a relationship expressing balance

misconceptions: equilibrium means the object must be at rest
constant speed alone is sufficient even if direction changes
questions: Can an object move while net force is zero?
What changes when one force no longer balances the other?
teacher_only.answer_visibility: Do not reveal missing force values or motion predictions in student diagrams before students reason them out.
teacher_only.worked_notes: Tie static and dynamic cases to the same zero-net-force condition.
teacher_only.wtc_interpretation: Use WTC to contrast equilibrium with a deliberately unbalanced modification.

sections.title: 1.5 Drawing Force Diagrams
sections.learning_target: Create and interpret simple force diagrams and use them to explain and predict motion.

student_facing.purpose: Integrate the unit by turning real interactions into a force-diagram model and using the model to explain motion.
concept_sequence: compare forces and determine net force
critique and revise incorrect force diagrams/explanations

worked_examples.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording, force diagram, and solution exactly at Stage 4B.

you_try.instruction: Copy canonical Bank wording and diagram exactly; preserve answer-hidden representation.

wtc.placement: after students have drawn and interpreted at least one complete force diagram
wtc.instruction: Use canonical wording exactly; preserve any flawed diagram/claim without answer-revealing annotations.

representation_progression: annotated model showing correct force ownership
item_lenses: every force arrow represents an external interaction on the chosen system
labels must identify forces, not objects or vague actions
diagram balance connects directly to net force and motion change

misconceptions: labeling an arrow with an object name instead of a force
drawing forces exerted by the system on other objects
adding a force in the direction of motion merely because the object moves
questions: Which external objects interact with it?
Is each arrow a force on the system?
What does the vector sum predict?
teacher_only.answer_visibility: Student figures must not contain answer-revealing labels when the task is to identify, label, classify, critique, or infer those features.
teacher_only.worked_notes: Model a repeatable system→interactions→arrows→net force→motion workflow.
teacher_only.wtc_interpretation: Use WTC as a critique task that tests force ownership and correct labeling, not just arithmetic.

global_rendering_constraints.bank_content: Canonical Bank wording, item structures, solutions, and representation-bearing figures must be copied exactly when referenced; Stage 4A does not rewrite them.
global_rendering_constraints.visual_priority: Bank representations outrank toolkit assets. Toolkit assets may support instruction but may not replace a required Bank representation.
global_rendering_constraints.toolkit: Course-owned Physics Notes Image Toolkit v3.1.0 at resources/Physics_Notes_Image_Toolkit/. No web images and no replacement drawings.
global_rendering_constraints.asset_size_rule: Static raster assets pass when width >= 900 px and height >= 550 px; otherwise use an approved animation asset when required by the PM.
global_rendering_constraints.student_answer_visibility: Do not place answer-revealing labels/annotations on student-facing figures for identification, labeling, classification, critique, or inference tasks.
global_rendering_constraints.math_and_concepts: Equations are relationships describing phenomena; conceptual reasoning comes before formula manipulation.
